claim: Federal Student Aid reported more than $1.7 trillion in outstanding federal student loans across 42.3 million recipients. More than 9.3 million recipients were in default with $234 billion outstanding, about 14% of the $1.64 trillion federally managed portfolio. About 3.5 million recipients in active repayment were more than 30 days delinquent, including about 1.5 million in late-stage delinquency.
scope: Federal student-loan portfolio; recipient counts can overlap across loan statuses. FSA warns that recent status comparisons are affected by the long payment pause, on-ramp, Fresh Start, and SAVE-related transitions.
source_title: Federal Student Aid Posts Updated Reports to FSA Data Center

claim: The Federal Reserve Bank of New York reported $1.651 trillion in student-loan balances on consumer credit reports in Q2 2026, down $7 billion from Q1. The annualized flow of student-loan balances into serious delinquency was 7.83% in Q2 2026.
scope: New York Fed Consumer Credit Panel / Equifax measure; this is not identical to FSA's federal-loan portfolio, so do not treat the two totals as competing estimates of exactly the same universe.
source_title: Household Debt Balances Decreased Slightly; Credit Card Delinquency Transition Rates Remained Steady

claim: Opportunity Insights found that at Ivy-Plus colleges (the eight Ivy League schools plus Duke, MIT, Stanford, and the University of Chicago), 14.5% of students came from the top 1% of the parental-income distribution, 13.5% from the bottom half, and 3.8% from the bottom quintile in its baseline cohorts.
scope: Historical linked-tax-data result for older cohorts, not a claim about the exact income distribution of students enrolled in 2026 and not an MIT-only estimate.
source_title: Income Segregation and Intergenerational Mobility Across Colleges in the United States

claim: Blackball treats study -> credential -> engineering occupation -> consequential engineering work as separate empirical transitions. It records education, demonstrated skill, hiring mechanism, work allocation, ownership/authority, material support, labor underneath design, and historical demand separately.

The MIT employment note separates target-job conversion from generic employment and separates outside employer demand from academic self-reproduction. It explicitly asks whether taking a compiler course, doing compiler laboratory work, or completing a master's actually converts into a compiler job.
Preserve the reported cases of an MIT-trained compiler candidate with a master's degree and substantial compiler work who could not obtain the expected compiler job.
scope: Named people and primary records are still required. Retrieve as a negative lead; do not present as a verified prevalence estimate or named case until the canonical MIT note is completed.

triggers: The Most Southern Place on Earth
claim: The Cobb/Turnbull node asks what a technically educated planter actually did, what property enabled the project, and who performed the physical work. Current evidence identifies Frederick G. Turnbull as a Princeton graduate who studied civil engineering and describes four Black men doing tree-cutting and flatboat construction while he organized the settlement.
scope: The source dossier marks this as an incomplete identification lead. The legal status of the four men and the remembered larger enslaved-person count are not yet verified.
source_title: James C. Cobb, The Most Southern Place on Earth: The Mississippi Delta and the Roots of Regional Identity

claim: Joel N. Shurkin's Broken Genius describes William Hillman Shockley, father of transistor co-inventor William B. Shockley, as an MIT-trained mining engineer from a prominent family who was a mediocre mathematics student, had trouble finding work, speculated in mines, and eventually worked for mining companies in California, Nevada, and London.
scope: This is a biographical counterexample to treating an MIT engineering credential as automatic evidence of stable occupational success. It is one case, not a labor-market rate.
source_title: Joel N. Shurkin, Broken Genius: The Rise and Fall of William Shockley, Creator of the Electronic Age, chapter 1, pp. 3-4

claim: Use Manuel Moreno Fraginals's The Sugarmill as a historical control against treating machinery or technical improvement as a complete account of production. The book analyzes sugar machinery and technical change inside a plantation economy organized around capital, land, workers, and slavery; retrieve it when a prestige narrative credits technical expertise while backgrounding the labor and ownership system.
scope: The bibliographic identity and subject matter are verified. Specific engineer-versus-worker passages should be attached at page level before being used as quotations or narrow factual claims.
source_title: Manuel Moreno Fraginals, The Sugarmill: The Socioeconomic Complex of Sugar in Cuba, 1760-1860

claim: The Harvard dossier treats Harvard as a credentialing, selection, sponsorship, and authority-conversion node rather than as proof of merit by itself. It keeps chronology separate from causation and asks what resources, sponsorship, networks, and occupational paths the institution actually supplied.
Preserve the reported case of an Uber driver with a master's degree in electrical engineering as a negative employment-conversion lead.
scope: No named person, date, school, or independent record is attached here. Do not turn this into a prevalence claim.

claim: Preserve the reported Ann Arbor climbing/robotics case of a chemistry PhD who did not obtain the expected chemistry career and instead worked in a summer-camp setting.
scope: Degree subfield and employment chronology remain to be pinned down. Use only as a retrieval lead until named records are attached.

claim: Preserve the previously collected battery-technology / chemical-engineering case as a negative lead for claims that technical novelty or engineering training automatically produces a stable career or valuable commercial outcome.
scope: Attach the named person, source, and chronology before using this as a factual case.

claim: In Opportunity Insights' historical college-mobility data, 15.4% of Harvard students came from families in the top 1% of the parental-income distribution, approximately the same share as from the bottom three quintiles combined.
scope: Historical cohort result from linked tax/college data; do not present it as the exact composition of Harvard students enrolled in 2026.
source_title: Income Segregation and Intergenerational Mobility Across Colleges in the United States

scope: Historical cohort result from linked tax/college data; do not present it as the exact composition of Berkeley students enrolled in 2026.
